caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: DANDI:001619
attempts.paper_title: A brainstem map of orofacial rhythms

inputs.what: Allen CCF structure tree (names, acronyms and parent regions), to map the files' region names to the regions the claims name.
The paper's analysis code, whose steps are ported in kaku.py (as the claims file adopts them); no data from it.
Allen CCFv3 annotation volume (2017 release, 25 um), to build the regions the CCF does not label (preBotzinger complex, parts of IRN, the areas next to AMB and NTS) as the claims file words them.

attempts.entry_title: A brainstem map of orofacial rhythms (Kaku, Liu et al. 2025)
attempts.summary: The paper's findings on licking and breathing held in part in this data, and its photostimulation, cued-task and paired-recording findings could not be tested, as the dandiset holds only the licking-task recordings. Breaths were delayed before slower licks, both rhythms resumed at fixed latencies after swallows, and licking units clustered in the hypoglossal and trigeminal nuclei and the IRN. Inspirations did not fall only between licks (30.4% came during a tongue protrusion), and the lick interval was not preserved across swallows. Licks were delayed before slower breaths over sessions but not over mice, and whether breathing units cluster near the preBötzinger complex could not be decided, as the paper does not define that region.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Kaku, Liu et al. (2025) on dandiset 001619, which holds the brainstem Neuropixels recordings of 31 mice in the multi-directional licking task, with DeepLabCut tracking of jaw and tongue, the airflow trace and CCF positions of the units. It ports the paper's analysis code to streamed NWB files and tests the lick-breath timing, swallow detection, unit counts, phase tuning to licking and breathing, swallow modulation and their maps. The cued licking task with photostimulation, the rat recordings, the raw videos and the premotor tracing are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Kaku, Liu et al. (2025) from dandiset 001619

outcomes.statement: The dandiset is the data the paper's analysis code reads, so that the code's choices fixed in this file apply to it.
outcomes.source: Code availability; the dandiset description; README of NuoLiLabBCM/KakuEtAl2025 at commit fbc0abe
outcomes.notes: Every input of process_mat.py is in the files (spike times per trial with the per-trial counts, the six quality metrics, CCF coordinates and region names, the 25 kHz airflow with timestamps and per-trial sample counts, side and bottom DLC jaw, tongue and lickport with likelihoods, 3D jaw, tongue and lickport tracks). get_good_units keeps 20,109 units over the 335 files, 0.9% below 20,300; with the Methods' drift metric added, 16,957 (16.5% below). All 173 sessions ran through the code's steps. The spike index must be read as start offsets (finding).
deviations: The files are read directly; the code's nwb2mat converter (a Windows MATLAB executable) was not used.

outcomes.statement: Across 339 insertions in 31 mice, 20,300 single units passed quality control (60 +- 22 per probe), 5,700 in the cerebellum, 3,700 in the pons and 10,900 in the medulla.
outcomes.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 2; Methods, Preprocessing, spike sorting, and quality metrics, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: we obtained 20,300 clear single units, including 5,700 units in the cerebellum, 3,700 units in the pons, and 10,900 units in the medulla
outcomes.notes: Code filter 20,109 units (tolerance 18,270 to 22,330), 60.0 per probe (SD 32.9 against 22), 31 mice; 335 insertions, not 339. Cerebellum 4,157 (5,385 with the arbor vitae, within tolerance), pons 3,021 and medulla 8,992, both below tolerance; 2,711 good units lie outside these regions, 1,222 of them in the arbor vitae and others in the cerebellar peduncles and the spinal tract of the trigeminal nerve. The criterion defines no partial outcome, and the insertions, the pons and the medulla are outside it, so the outcome is not reproduced (changed from partially reproduced after round 3); the total, the mean per probe and the mice match. Whether fibre-tract units belong to a division is asked of a reader (questions/kaku-2025.yaml); it does not change the outcome, since the insertion count fails. With the drift metric 16,957 units (CB 3,292, P 2,698, MY 7,626).
deviations: Regions are taken from the Allen structure tree (iblatlas copy, pinned) by the unit's region name; whether the paper counts the arbor vitae as cerebellum is not stated, and both counts are shown.

outcomes.statement: Neurons in the cerebellum (22 +- 29 spikes/s) and vestibular nucleus (38 +- 32) fired faster than neurons in the medulla (11 +- 14).
outcomes.source: Methods, Preprocessing, spike sorting, and quality metrics, paragraph 2; Figure 2e
outcomes.quote: Neurons in the cerebellum and the vestibular nucleus exhibited higher spike rates than neurons in the medulla (22 ± 29 spikes/s, mean ± std, for cerebellum, 38 ± 32 spikes/s for vestibular nucleus, and 11 ± 14 spikes/s for medulla
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), avg_firing_rate: cerebellum 21.3 +- 28.8 (n 4,157), vestibular nuclei 27.2 +- 28.8 (n 1,276), medulla without VNC 10.9 +- 14.5 (n 7,716), with VNC 13.2. Reading (b), spikes in the first 5 s of good trials: 21.4, 27.2, 11.3 and 13.6. Cerebellum and medulla (ii) are within tolerance; the vestibular nuclei are not (38 +- 3.8) under any reading, though they still fire faster than the medulla. The criterion asks for all three means under one reading and defines no partial outcome, so the outcome is not reproduced (changed from partially reproduced after round 1).
deviations: Reading (b) uses spikes in the code's analysis window (the first 5.0014 s of each good trial) over that time, since the trials carry no session times.

outcomes.statement: Mice licked at 6.23 +- 2 Hz (95% range 3.59 to 8.91 Hz) and breathed at lower frequencies, 4.02 +- 1.24 Hz (95% range 2.12 to 7.17 Hz).
outcomes.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 2; Figure 1d
outcomes.quote: Licking occurred at 6.23 ± 2 Hz (mean ± std, 95% range: 3.59 - 8.91 Hz) while breathing occurred at lower frequencies (4.02 ± 1.24 Hz, 95% range: 2.12 - 7.17 Hz; Figure 1d)
outcomes.notes: Reading (b), within one lick bout: licking 6.07 +- 1.08 Hz (95% range 3.77 to 8.40), breathing 4.19 +- 1.01 Hz (2.41 to 6.39); both means and both licking bounds are within tolerance, the breathing bounds are not (2.12 +- 0.21, 7.17 +- 0.72). Reading (a), within trials: licking 26.96 Hz (1.11 to 147.06), breathing 3.89 Hz (2.10 to 6.68), all three breathing values within tolerance. Round 1 counted under (b) onset pairs lying in two adjacent bouts (13,498 pairs), which gave 8.06 Hz; reading (b) now takes only pairs inside one bout, which changes the outcome from not reproduced. Under (a) 39,027 lick intervals are shorter than 2 frames (tongue detection flickering between frames); without them the mean under (a) is still 21.36 Hz (97.5th percentile 98 Hz). The code builds bouts from runs of lick intervals between 3 and 9 Hz, so the licking mean and range under (b) are largely fixed by that definition.
deviations: measured gives reading (b), the reading under which both means are within tolerance.

outcomes.statement: Inspiration always occurred between licks and never coincided with licking; licking preceded inspiration at a fixed latency.
outcomes.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 2; Figure 1f
outcomes.quote: Inspiration always occurred between licks and thus never coincided with licking. Licking preceded inspiration at a fixed latency
outcomes.notes: 70,298 of 231,563 in-bout inspiration onsets (30.4%) fall between a tongue onset and the next tongue offset; per session 3.3% to 46.1% (median 30.0%), per subject 8.5% to 42.5%; no session has none, so readings (a) and (b) both fail. The median latency from the last lick in a cycle to the next inspiration is 133 ms (1 lick), 92 ms (2), 82 ms (3) and 109 ms (4). The airflow-tongue cross-correlation peaks at 54 to 112 ms in 28 of 31 subjects (about 250 ms, the next cycle, in the other 3), with weak correlations (r 0.035 to 0.106). The six subjects with the lowest fractions, DL029 to DL034 (8.5% to 14.6%, against 22% to 42%), peak later (tongue 88.4 to 112.2 ms, median 103.7, against 54.4 to 95.2, median 78.2, in the 22 other first-cycle subjects; Mann-Whitney p = 0.00054), and over subjects the fraction falls as the lag rises (Spearman rho = -0.67, p = 0.00011). Moving each subject's inspirations earlier by its lag minus 78.2 ms raises DL029 to DL034 to 10.3% to 21.0% and gives 30.7% pooled, so the between-subject difference is consistent with a clock offset of 20 to 30 ms in those subjects, and no such correction brings the fraction near 0 or 5%.
deviations: A protrusion is taken from each tongue onset to the first tongue offset after it, both as the code detects them (likelihood > 0.95 in both views); the paper does not define the interval.

outcomes.statement: For breath cycles with two licks, the second lick was delayed preceding a slower breath compared to a fast breath, in all mice (one-sample t-test, two-tailed, p < 0.001), so breathing influences the licking rhythm.
outcomes.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 2; Figure 1g
outcomes.quote: In all mice, the lick timing was significantly delayed preceding a slower breath compared to a fast breath (Figure 1g, p<0.001, one sample t-test, two-tailed)
outcomes.notes: 71 of 173 sessions give a value (83 have at least 40 two-lick cycles per half; the others lack a peak in a window). Reading (a), sessions: mean 22.0 ms, t = 3.68, p = 4.5e-4. Reading (b), mice: mean 13.6 ms, p = 0.18 (n = 20). 16 of 20 mice have a positive mean, 1 zero and 3 negative (DL008 -120 ms from one session, DL011 -50, DL027 -33). 60 sessions are positive, 6 zero, 5 negative. A random split of the same cycles also gives a positive difference, because the slow window starts 40 ms after the fast one: 15.7 ms over 83 sessions with one split each (p = 0.0072); the data exceed the mean of 20 splits by 13.3 ms (paired p = 0.037, 54 of 71 sessions above the null; over mice 14 of 20 above it, paired p = 0.98). So the measured difference is separated from this artefact over sessions but not over mice. Of DL029 to DL034 only DL031 has a value (one session, 0 ms). The round-1 revision printed 18.3 ms, 9.1 ms and p = 0.17; the re-run for round 2 on another runner gives the values above (see the round-2 response). The outcome follows the criterion, which compares with 0.

outcomes.statement: During slow breathing, licking frequency increased abruptly to add licks within the breathing cycle (1, 2, 3 or 4 licks between breaths), keeping the fixed lick latency before the next inspiration, so licking shifted between modes of oscillation with breathing frequency.
outcomes.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 3; Figure 1f
outcomes.quote: During slow breathing, when the next lick could not be delayed further to accommodate the next breath, licking frequency abruptly increased to add additional licks within the breathing cycle to maintain the fixed lick latency preceding the next inspiration
outcomes.notes: The median inter-breath interval rises from 1 to 2 to 3 licks per cycle in 116 of 117 sessions that have all three (median session medians 0.228, 0.296, 0.418 s; 4 licks 0.558 s), so licks are added as breathing slows. The latency from the last lick to the next inspiration differs by 62.5% between the groups (pooled medians 133, 92 and 82 ms), and only 1 of 117 sessions keeps it within 20%, so the fixed-latency part fails. The criterion asks for both parts and defines no partial outcome (changed from partially reproduced after round 1).

outcomes.statement: Inspirations following licking were significantly delayed for slower licking frequencies, anticipating the next lick (one-sample t-test, two-tailed, p < 0.001), so licking influences breathing.
outcomes.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 4; Figure 1i
outcomes.quote: inspirations following licking were significantly delayed for slower licking frequencies to anticipate the next lick (Figure 1i, p<0.001, one sample t-test, two-tailed)
outcomes.notes: 86 sessions give a value. Reading (a): mean 10.5 ms, t = 6.79, p = 1.5e-9; reading (b), 23 mice: 9.6 ms, p = 0.0012. 44 sessions positive, 37 zero (the PSTH bins are 20 ms), 5 negative; 18 of 23 mice positive. Random-split null 2.7 ms (one split per session, p = 0.12); the data exceed the mean of 20 splits by 10.6 ms (paired p = 2.1e-10; 19 of 23 mice above it), so the effect is not an artefact of the two windows.

outcomes.statement: Neither a free-running breathing oscillator that sets lick timing nor a free-running licking oscillator that sets breath timing reproduces the observed lick-breath relationship, suggesting that the two oscillators are bidirectionally coupled.
outcomes.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 4; Extended Data Figure 1d-i; Methods, Simulation of licking-breathing coupling
outcomes.quote: This pattern of lick-breath temporal relationship also cannot be produced by a free-running licking oscillator unidirectionally setting the timing of breathing rhythm
outcomes.notes: Inter-breath intervals from fig1d reading (a), inter-lick intervals from reading (b) (within one bout), the readings closest to the paper for each rhythm; ranges 0.150 to 0.476 s and 0.119 to 0.265 s (2.5th to 97.5th percentiles); latencies 112 ms (last lick to inspiration) and 119 ms (inspiration to next lick). Breathing-driven model: Fig 1i difference 0.0 ms in all 162 of 172 simulated sessions with a value (no variance, so no test). Licking-driven model: a Fig 1g value in 1 of 172 sessions; 145 have at least 40 two-lick cycles per half, but the lick PSTH has a peak above threshold in the fast window in 18 and in the slow window in 12, since simulated licks do not lock to inspiration. So the licking-driven result holds because the measure is missing, not because a test found no effect. Data: 22.0 and 10.5 ms, both p < 0.001. The breathing-driven model gives a Fig 1g effect (59.3 ms, 141 sessions) and the licking-driven model a Fig 1i effect (35.9 ms, 169 sessions).
deviations: Simulated sessions match the data sessions in the number of in-bout inspirations (breathing model) or licks (licking model); sessions with fewer than 50 in-bout inspirations are skipped.

Licks are added evenly inside inter-lick intervals longer than the 97.5th percentile (breathing model), and an inspiration is omitted when it would follow the previous one by less than the 2.5th percentile inter-breath interval (licking model); the Methods describe both steps without numbers.

outcomes.statement: Licking and breathing in freely moving rats showed a similar lick-breath temporal relationship.
outcomes.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 4; Extended Data Figure 2
outcomes.quote: Independent analysis of breathing and licking in freely moving rats yielded similar temporal relationship (Extended Data Figure 2)
outcomes.notes: The rat lickometer and thermocouple recordings are not in the dandiset, and the paper names no deposit for them.

outcomes.statement: Licking was paused during detected swallows but not during ordinary expirations, so the detected events are genuine swallows.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 1b-c; Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Licking was paused during swallowing. Bottom, lick timing aligned to all expirations as a control. Lick was not paused during expiration.
outcomes.notes: 90 sessions with at least 20 swallows. Tongue-onset probability per 3.4 ms bin, 0 to 100 ms after onset: 0.0308 around swallows against 0.0211 around in-bout expiration onsets (median ratio 1.50); lower around swallows in 4 of 90 sessions; Wilcoxon p = 4.0e-16 in the opposite direction. The full trace shows the pause before the onset: from -90 to 0 ms 0.0036 to 0.0068 per bin (minimum 0.0026 at -48 ms) against about 0.021 around expirations; licking resumes from 0 to 60 ms (0.030 and 0.050). The detector keeps swallows with a lick within 0.25 s after the detected peak and takes the onset at the start of the airflow pause, so the window after onset favours licks. Whether the criterion's window misreads the paper is asked of a reader (questions/kaku-2025.yaml).
deviations: Expiration onset is the Hilbert phase (code filter, plus pi) wrapping through 2 pi, the claims file's choice.

outcomes.statement: Inspirations and licks followed swallowing at relatively fixed latencies despite different breath and lick timing before the swallow, suggesting that swallowing interrupted the ongoing rhythms.
outcomes.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 5; Figure 1k and 1m
outcomes.quote: Inspirations and licks followed swallowing at relatively fixed latencies despite different breath and lick timing before the swallow (Figure 1k and m)
outcomes.notes: 6,644 swallow events; 5,797 kept for licks, 6,300 for breaths (code selection). Licks: latency difference between top and bottom thirds 17.0 ms against cycle -1 differences of 27.2 (ranking O5 a) and 40.8 ms (b). Breaths: 37.4 and 23.8 ms against 95.2 and 122.4 ms.

outcomes.statement: The inter-lick interval before and after swallowing was preserved (one-sample t-test, two-tailed, P = 0.649).
outcomes.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 5; Figure 1l
outcomes.quote: The inter-lick-interval before and after swallowing was preserved (Figure 1l, P=0.649, one-sampled t-test, two-tailed)
outcomes.notes: Code selection (O5 a, 1,932 events): Delta(1,-1) = 119.5 ms, one-sample t-test p < 0.0001, so the paper's test finds a change. Variants: (b) 86.2 ms, (c) 50.3 ms (5,797 events), (d) 87.3 ms over 140 sessions, all p < 0.0001. The mean is driven by pauses after the swallow: cycle 1 exceeds 333 ms in 270 of 1,932 events (95th percentile 1,256 ms; cycle -1 never does), and the median Delta(1,-1) is 0.0 ms. Without those events (a diagnostic) the mean is -16.3 ms, p = 3e-24. The port computes cycle 1 as the paper's code does (generate_figures.plot_licking_swallow_summary, after_2 - after_1, no limit on cycle 1), checked against the code at fbc0abe.

outcomes.statement: The lick cycle in which swallowing occurred was significantly prolonged, by 33.3 ms (one-sample t-test, two-tailed, P < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 5; Figure 1l
outcomes.quote: whereas the lick cycle in which swallowing occurred was significantly prolonged by 33.3 ms (Figure 1l, P<0.001, one-sampled t-test, two-tailed)
outcomes.notes: Code selection (O5 a): Delta(0,-1) = 33.31 ms, p < 0.0001, n = 1,932. Other readings: (b) 3.9 ms, (c) 11.0 ms, (d) 38.8 ms, all p < 0.0001. The selection of the longest cycles 0 favours a positive value, as the claims file notes.

outcomes.statement: The inter-breath interval before and after swallowing was preserved (P = 0.225).
outcomes.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 5; Figure 1n
outcomes.quote: P=0.225 for inter-breath-interval before vs. after swallowing
outcomes.notes: Code selection (O5 a, 2,100 events): Delta(1,-1) = -2.1 ms, p = 0.20. Variants: (c) -0.9 ms, p = 0.26; (b) -25.3 ms, p < 0.0001; (d) -6.6 ms, p = 0.0099 over 135 sessions.

outcomes.statement: The breath cycle in which swallowing occurred was significantly prolonged, by 48.0 ms (one-sample t-test, two-tailed, P < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, Coordination of breathing, licking, and swallowing, paragraph 5; Figure 1n
outcomes.quote: P<0.001 for inter-breath-interval in which swallowing occurred, one-sample t-test, two-tailed, prolonged by 48.0 ms

outcomes.statement: Units showed significant phase tuning to licking (3551 of 20,300) or breathing (1015 of 20,300), but rarely to both (182 of 20,300).
outcomes.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Individual units exhibited significant phase tuning to either licking (3551/20300), or breathing (1015/20300), but rarely to both (182/20300)
outcomes.notes: Counts with licking and breathing including the units tuned to both (i). V3(a): order 4 3,517 / 1,023 / 178; order 2 3,583 / 1,036 / 196; code order 5 3,500 / 1,026 / 177; all within tolerance of 3,551 / 1,015 / 182. The code's 100-resample scheme gives the same (3,515 / 1,023 / 178 at order 4). V3(b): order 4 2,759 / 602 / 69, order 2 2,805 / 605 / 70, outside. Under (ii) no reading matches. As the criterion asks for every reading of V3, the counts do not hold; the partial rule holds under every reading (both-tuned 2.5% to 5.5% of licking units, 11.5% to 18.9% of breathing units). V3(b) ranks the measured MI against random-phase MIs, which for noisy units are often as large as the measured one; V3(a) compares resampled-spike MIs with random-phase MIs, as the Methods' rank-sum test and the code do.
deviations: The 1000 resampled tuning curves per unit are fitted by a grid search over width and preferred phase with amplitude and baseline in closed form, not curve_fit; the measured MI uses curve_fit as the code. On 300 random units the two fits differ by a median of 0.0015 in MI and fall on the same side of 0.6 in 99%; on 24 units with MI > 0.6 the code's 100-resample test gives the same decision with either fit.
Resampled histograms are drawn as multinomials on the measured histogram's bins, which has the distribution of the code's resampling; the code's bin edges follow each resample's range.
Significance resamples are computed only for units whose measured MI exceeds 0.6, the only units that can count.

outcomes.statement: Of 18,485 units, 427 were modulated by swallowing only, 175 by both licking and swallowing and 55 by both breathing and swallowing.
outcomes.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 3; Extended Data Figure 5e-f
outcomes.quote: Most units were modulated by swallowing only (427/18485), with a smaller group modulated by both licking and swallowing (175/18485) (Extended Data Figure 5f). Another small subset of units with swallowing-related activity were also modulated by breathing (55/18485)
outcomes.notes: Denominator reading (a), units of sessions with a swallow: 18,494 (paper 18,485); reading (b), units with at least 20 swallows: 10,807. Swallow-modulated units: 525 under V4(a), 362 under V4(b). V4(a) with order 4, V3(a): swallow only 264 (i) or 319 (ii), licking and swallowing 206, breathing and swallowing 87; other tuning readings give 262 to 355, 170 to 212 and 65 to 87. V4(b): 187 to 264, 98 to 126 and 62 to 84. No combination puts the three counts within tolerance of 427, 175 and 55.

outcomes.statement: Units encoding breathing clustered near the preBotzinger complex and in the posterior ventral IRN.
outcomes.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 4; Figure 2f
outcomes.quote: Units encoding breathing were near the preBötzinger complex 22, as well as posterior ventral IRN
outcomes.notes: The two readings of AMB's extent in O3 give different outcomes, which the claims file's header blocks (changed from reproduced after round 3). The preBotzinger complex is built from the CCF annotation: within 300 or 500 um below AMB, inside the whole nucleus's AP and ML extent (AP 11,350 to 12,575, |ML| 1,225 to 1,525, ventral edge DV 6,750 um), it holds 36 and 41 good units, 20 or 21 breathing-tuned (49% to 58%), against 4.4% to 6.7% of pons and medulla units, Fisher p < 0.0001. With AMB's ML extent and ventral edge taken in each 100 um AP step, it holds 12 or 15 units, 2 or 3 tuned, p 0.04 to 0.27, and 4 of the 10 combinations of tuning reading and distance fail. The whole-nucleus box takes AMB's deepest point and full ML range at every AP level, so a unit can count as within 300 um below AMB where it lies further below the local nucleus; the paper gives no numbers for the region. Posterior ventral IRN holds 88 to 109 of 517 tuned units (17% to 21%), p < 0.0001, under every reading. Round 1 built the box from 87 AMB-labelled units (16 units, p 0.0004 to 0.0032). The box's units come from 10 mice in 12 sessions (at most 10 or 12 from DL009), its 21 tuned units (order 4, V3 a) from 7 mice (at most 6 from one); the per-step reading has 12 or 15 units in 5 mice.
deviations: AMB's "anterior-posterior and medial-lateral extent" in O3 is read both as the extent of the whole nucleus in the CCF annotation and as its extent in each 100 um AP step. Regions come from the Allen CCFv3 2017 annotation at 25 um (inputs), whose label at the unit's position equals the file's region name for 96.3% of good units.

outcomes.statement: Licking-related units were broadly distributed, including the hypoglossal (12N) and trigeminal (5N) motor nuclei, extensive portions of the IRN and parts of the pons.
outcomes.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 4; Figure 2g
outcomes.quote: The regions containing licking-related activity were remarkably broad, including the tongue- and jaw-related motor nuclei (hypoglossal nucleus, 12N; trigeminal nucleus, 5N) as well as extensive portions of the IRN and parts of pons
outcomes.notes: Licking-tuned fractions: XII 36% to 45% (166 units), V 43% to 55% (269), IRN 34% to 40% (1,804), against 20% to 26% of pons and medulla units, Fisher p < 0.00001 in each under every reading; pons 15% to 20% of 3,021 units, above 1%.

outcomes.statement: Swallowing-related units clustered in the trigeminal nucleus (5N), lateral to the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) and above the nucleus ambiguus (10N), with further clusters in the inferior colliculus and the nucleus of the lateral lemniscus.
outcomes.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 4; Figure 2h; Extended Data Figure 6a-d
outcomes.quote: Units with swallowing-related activity were clustered in the trigeminal nucleus (5N), lateral to the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS), and above the nucleus ambiguus (10N)
outcomes.notes: The two readings of V4 give different outcomes, which the claims file's header blocks. V4(a): enriched in V (13 of 234, 5.6%, p = 0.018), IC (10.9%), NLL (10.1%) and above AMB (8.7% and 7.6%, p = 0.005 and 0.002) against 2.8% in the same sessions, not lateral of NTS (1.9% to 2.0%): four of five under both distances, partially reproduced. V4(b): V 3.4% (p = 0.095), IC and NLL enriched, above AMB 4.3% (p = 0.11) at 300 um and 4.5% (p = 0.037) at 500 um: two and three of five, not reproduced. Regions from the CCF annotation (see fig2f). Round 1 adopted V4(a) as an assumption; the verifier pointed to the header's rule, and the outcome was changed from partially reproduced. The question of the normalisation is put to the authors (findings).
deviations: "Lateral of NTS" is units beyond the lateral edge of NTS in the CCF annotation in the same 100 um AP step, within the distance; "above AMB" is units within the distance above AMB's dorsal edge inside its AP and ML extent.

outcomes.statement: Swallow-related activity in 5N and IRN leads swallowing, while activity in the inferior colliculus and nucleus of the lateral lemniscus follows it.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 6e; Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: Activities in 5N and IRN lead swallowing while activities in the IC and NLL follow swallowing.
outcomes.notes: Median PSTH peak time (within +-0.15 s) of swallow-modulated units: V and IRN -1 ms (111 units, V4 a) and -4 ms (68, V4 b); IC and NLL +16 ms (53 and 45 units); Mann-Whitney p < 0.0001 under both. By region (V4 a): V -11 ms (13), IRN -1 ms (98), IC +13 ms (34), NLL +20 ms (19). The lead of IRN is small, within one video frame.

outcomes.statement: A GLM on the tracked features found separate clusters of units predicted by licking or by breathing movements.
outcomes.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 5; Extended Data Figure 7c-d
outcomes.quote: The GLM found separate clusters of units predicted by either licking or breathing movement (Extended Data Figure 7c-d)
outcomes.notes: Not run. The notebook times the unpenalised GLM (O8 a, log link) on one session: one lag for its 176 units takes 36.2 s in the executed copy of this revision (0.205 s per unit; 25.8 s in the copy the verifier reviewed in round 2). For 20,109 units and 11 lags that is about 12.6 CPU hours (9.0 in the earlier copy), 25.2 with the logit link, and at least 151.5 with the five penalty values of O8 (b), against a 60-minute limit for the notebook. The claim needs every reading of O8, so a subset or one reading cannot give its outcome, and none was run.

outcomes.statement: The autoencoder embedding predicted a larger fraction of activity variance than the tracked features for most units across the brainstem (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, Brainstem activity maps of orofacial rhythms, paragraph 6; Extended Data Figure 7g

findings.statement: In all 335 files units/spike_times_index holds the offset where each unit's spikes start, not where they end as NWB requires; standard readers (pynwb) therefore give every unit the spikes of the unit before it. The per-unit, per-trial spike counts in 'unit and trial pairs' agree with the start-offset reading in every file.
findings.checked: reproduce_kaku_2025.ipynb cell 6 prints that spike_times_index read as start offsets matches the per-trial spike counts in 335 of 335 files and read as end offsets in 0. The test runs in a helper module, so only the summary count is printed, and the pynwb behaviour is stated in markdown and follows from the index layout; it was not run.

findings.statement: In 19 files the units/histology table (region and CCF position) has more rows than the units (for example 680 against 613 in DL034 session 20220205 probe p2), so its rows cannot be matched to units with certainty; the paper's code, and this attempt, take them by position.

The subject age field reads P210W to P303W (210 to 303 weeks) for every file, which does not fit adult mice in an acute recording study; the general/stimulus field says 'photostim' in every file, but no file holds photostimulation or cue data.

The 'left'/'right' hemisphere text of unit_location and of the insertion's recordable_brain_regions puts 99.3% of units on the side opposite to the one ccf_x gives if it increases to the right (midline 5,700 um); the files do not name the CCF axes or their direction, so the side of a unit cannot be fixed.

The 3D tracking's idx field matches the DLC trial number in 154 of 173 sessions and the trial number minus one in 19 sessions (15 subjects), judged by the correlation of the 2D and 3D tongue tracks (median 0.98 at the matching offset); the files do not say how idx counts trials.
findings.checked: reproduce_kaku_2025.ipynb cell 11 prints offset 0 as best in 154 sessions and offset -1 in 19 sessions, with 15 subjects listed for -1 and a median correlation of 0.983 at the offset used. The evidence is a summary of 2D against 3D track correlations with a minimum of 0.354 at the chosen offset, so a few sessions are assigned with weak support, but a reader who takes idx as the trial number pairs the 3D tracks with the wrong trial in one of the two groups.

findings.statement: The 3D tracking (jaw_side, tongue_bottom, lickport_bottom) has no stated axes, origin or units, and the trial tables have no target position, so the lick direction of Extended Data Fig 8 cannot be computed; along the 3D x axis licking units prefer opposite sides in the two hemispheres, but which side is ipsilateral cannot be named.

Every trial in the trial tables starts at 0 and spikes, tracking and airflow are stored per trial relative to its start, so trials cannot be placed on one session clock and inter-trial periods are absent.

In every two-probe session (162) the airflow and DLC tracking of the two files are the same recording deposited twice (identical samples and lengths). The 3D tracking holds one trial fewer than the trial table in 211 files, and the side-camera DLC rows differ from trials x 1471 in 25 files.

In six subjects (DL029 to DL034) the airflow-tongue cross-correlation peaks 20 to 30 ms later than in the other subjects (tongue lag median 103.7 against 78.2 ms), and fewer in-bout inspirations fall inside a tongue protrusion (8.5% to 14.6% against 22% to 42%). The files do not say how the airflow and video clocks were aligned, so a per-subject offset between them cannot be excluded.

The dandiset holds only the multi-directional licking task recordings (335 insertions, where the paper reports 339). The cued licking task, the ALM, latSC and brainstem photostimulation experiments, the rat recordings, the raw videos used by the autoencoder and the premotor tracing data are not in it, and the paper names no other deposit; 18 of the 48 claims are blocked for missing data.

The assumption is stated, but the whole-nucleus box is not clearly better than the per-AP-step reading: it takes AMB's deepest point (DV 6,750 um) and full ML range across all AP levels, so a unit can count as within 300 um ventral of AMB where it lies more than 300 um below the local nucleus. The outcome flips between the two readings (36 or 41 units, p < 0.0001, against 12 or 15, p 0.04 to 0.27), and the header blocks a claim whose region readings disagree. I recommend blocked, methods_underspecified. At the least, the record should show how many mice the units come from.

paper_notes.statement: The Methods list a drift metric < 0.5 among the unit filters and a 4-pole Butterworth filter for phase tuning; the paper's code applies no drift filter and uses a 5th-order filter. The code's filter gives 20,109 units, close to the paper's 20,300; with the drift metric it gives 16,957.

Question for the authors (fig2-licking-breathing-tuned-counts): the Methods compare the measured MI against 1000 MIs from resampled phases with a Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Is the test between MIs of resampled spike phases and MIs of random session phases (as process_mat.py does, 100 of each), or of the measured MI against the random-phase MIs? The first reproduces 3,517 / 1,021 / 177 tuned units here, the second 2,757 / 602 / 69.

Question for the authors (fig2h-swallow-units-location, fig2-swallow-modulated-counts): is the swallow MI normalised by the larger of the two window rates (the code) or by the peak of the swallow PSTH (the Methods' 'peak spike rate during swallowing')? Here the first gives three of five enriched regions, the second two. Neither reproduces the counts 427 / 175 / 55; how were swallow-only units defined?

Question for the authors (fig2f, ed8bc, fig4d, fig4e, fig4f): how were units 'near the preBotzinger complex' and in 'posterior-dorsal IRN/PARN' selected, since the CCF does not label them, and which 43 recordings form Fig 4d? With a region below AMB inside the nucleus's whole extent (CCF annotation) 36 to 41 units qualify and 2 or 3 recordings; with AMB's extent per AP step, 12 to 15 units and the enrichment of fig2f and ed8bc is lost.

Question for the authors (fig1g, fig4e): the peak windows of get_peak_diff_lick_behv and get_peak_diff_lick_unit start 40 and 60 ms later for the slow half than for the fast half. On these data a random split of the same cycles gives a positive slow-minus-fast difference (15.7 ms for Fig 1g, 47 to 55 ms for Fig 4e), close to the measured one. Was the difference compared with a split at random, or with equal windows?

entries.name: kaku-2025
entries.title: A brainstem map of orofacial rhythms (Kaku, Liu et al. 2025)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Kaku, Liu et al. (2025) on dandiset 001619, which holds the brainstem Neuropixels recordings of 31 mice in the multi-directional licking task, with DeepLabCut tracking of jaw and tongue, the airflow trace and CCF positions of the units. It ports the paper's analysis code to streamed NWB files and tests the lick-breath timing, swallow detection, unit counts, phase tuning to licking and breathing, swallow modulation and their maps. The cued licking task with photostimulation, the rat recordings, the raw videos and the premotor tracing are not in the dandiset.
